title: Chiral superconductors from parent states with non-uniform Berry curvature: Momentum-space vortices, BdG topology, and thermal Hall conductivity
summary: We investigate chiral superconductivity emerging from parent electronic states with non-uniform Berry curvature, motivated by recent experiments in rhombohedral graphene multilayers. Using the continuum $λ_N$-model-a tunable platform with independently controllable Berry curvature profiles-we solve the full BCS gap equation on a continuum Chern band beyond the weak-coupling limit. We find that a non-uniform Berry curvature of the parent band enriches the superconducting order parameter, leading to the formation of momentum-space vortices in the gap function away from high-symmetry points. By tuning the Berry curvature profile, we identify distinct regimes associated with vortex nucleation and vortex number saturation, and show that the nucleation of momentum-space vortices tends to lower the condensation energy. We then show analytically that the parent band Chern number constrains the number of momentum-space vortices that can nucleate in the gap-independent of details of the $λ_N$-model. We also provide a gauge-invariant formulation for computing the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Berry curvature for continuum models, and find that it is determined by a momentum-space phase current. The winding of this current around vortices in the occupied region in turn determines the BdG Chern number. Finally, we discuss how thermal Hall measurements can be used to probe the formation of momentum-space vortices. Our results highlight the crucial role of Berry curvature in shaping chiral superconductivity, and offer guiding principles for its identification in systems such as rhombohedral graphene.

AI.tldr: Non-uniform Berry curvature in a continuum Chern band drives formation of momentum-space vortices in a chiral superconducting gap; vortex nucleation lowers condensation energy, is constrained by the parent-band Chern number, and can be probed via thermal Hall response—relevant to rhombohedral graphene.
AI.method: Solve the full BCS gap equation beyond weak coupling on a tunable continuum λ_N-model with controllable Berry-curvature profiles; derive analytic constraint linking parent-band Chern number to allowed vortex number; develop a gauge-invariant BdG Berry-curvature formulation expressed via a momentum-space phase current.
AI.tags: quantum_geometry, topology, vortex, chiral_superconductivity, BdG, berry_curvature, Chern_number, rhombohedral_graphene

title: Tunneling spectra of $\mathrm{TaO}_x$ junctions for van der Waals superconductors
summary: Tunneling spectroscopy and its evolution are crucial for elucidating the intricate electronic structure and emergent phenomena in quantum materials.Nevertheless, high-quality measurements -- specifically those tracking evolution across temperature and external fields -- remain a formidable challenge. We have fabricated a high-quality $\mathrm{TaO}_x$-based planar tunneling junction by using magnetron sputtering for van der Waals (vdW) superconductors. Using the vdW superconductor $\mathrm{Bi}_2\mathrm{Sr}_2\mathrm{CaCu}_2\mathrm{O}_{8+δ}$ (Bi2212) as a benchmark, this platform yields high-quality tunneling spectra, reproducing the electronic signatures obtained from scanning tunneling spectra acquired from atomically clean surfaces under ultra-high vacuum conditions. This architecture enables high-precision spectroscopy across extensive temperature and magnetic field ranges, offering a universal strategy for probing the electronic structures of diverse two-dimensional systems and facilitating future explorations of material properties.

AI.tldr: Developed a TaOx-based planar tunneling-junction platform (fabricated by magnetron sputtering) for van der Waals superconductors. Benchmarking on Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8+δ reproduces high-quality STM-like tunneling spectra and enables high-precision spectroscopy across wide temperature and magnetic-field ranges, offering a universal probe for 2D quantum materials.
AI.method: Fabrication of planar TaOx tunneling junctions by magnetron sputtering on vdW superconductors; tunneling spectroscopy measurements as a function of temperature and magnetic field on Bi2212 and comparison to STM/STS benchmarks.
AI.tags: superconductivity, tunneling_spectroscopy, quantum_devices, van_der_Waals_superconductors, device_fabrication, TaOx, Bi2212, magnetron_sputtering, magnetic_field_dependence, temperature_dependence

title: Quasiparticle GW for Superconductors: Toward a Unified Treatment of Electron-Phonon and Electron-Plasmon Couplings
summary: Superconducting two-dimensional materials, and in particular few-layer graphene, offer an exciting platform for low-power electronics, yet the origin of their unconventional superconductivity remains an open question. Prevailing theories, primarily rooted in the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) framework that assumes electron-phonon interactions are the main mechanism of superconductivity, struggle to account quantitatively for the observed phenomena. Recent studies point to a plasmonic pairing mechanism in graphene systems; however, disentangling the relative contributions of phonon- and plasmon-mediated pairing remains challenging due to the lack of a satisfactory first-principles framework capable of accurately capturing dynamical screening effects in the electronic channel. Here, we present a new theoretical framework that extends the quasiparticle self-consistent GW method to the superconducting phase by coupling it with the Eliashberg treatment of both phonon- and plasmon-mediated interactions. Our approach, termed "s-qpGW", is on par with the state-of-the-art Eliashberg theory of superconductivity when applied to bulk metals, and correctly predicts the absence of superconductivity in doped monolayer graphene. To differentiate s-qpGW from conventional Eliashberg approaches, we study a simple model system, graphene with an artificially enhanced density of states, and demonstrate that s-qpGW captures dynamical Coulomb screening effects in ways that standard BCS theory cannot.

AI.tldr: Introduces s-qpGW, a superconducting extension of quasiparticle self-consistent GW coupled to Eliashberg equations including both phonon- and plasmon-mediated pairing. The method reproduces state-of-the-art Eliashberg results for bulk metals, correctly finds no superconductivity in doped monolayer graphene, and captures dynamical Coulomb screening effects beyond standard BCS in a model graphene system with enhanced density of states.
AI.method: Coupling quasiparticle self-consistent GW (qpGW) to superconducting Eliashberg theory to treat phonon and plasmon pairing channels on equal footing, thereby incorporating first-principles dynamical Coulomb screening in the electronic pairing interaction (method named “s-qpGW”). Benchmarked against bulk metals and applied to monolayer/model graphene.
AI.tags: superconductivity, plasmonic_pairing, Eliashberg, quasiparticle_self-consistent_GW, dynamical_screening, graphene, 2D_superconductors

title: Anomalous acoustoelectric signatures of chiral superconductivity
summary: The identification of unconventional pairing in two-dimensional materials is a central challenge in modern condensed matter physics. While chiral p-wave superconductivity offers a promising platform for topological quantum computing, its detection remains elusive due to the inherent limitations of optical probes in the two-dimensional limit. We propose the anomalous acoustoelectric effect as a robust, alternative to optical signature of p-wave paring symmetry. We demonstrate that an acoustic wave induces a transverse dc current resulting in a measurable condensate phase difference on sample boundaries originating from the anisotropic scattering of quasiparticles in the absence of an external magnetic field. Crucially, the quasiparticle-mediated acoustoelectric response dominates near the critical temperature and, unlike the superconducting condensate, is not suppressed by electron-hole asymmetry factor. These results establish the anomalous acoustoelectric effect as a high-sensitivity electrical probe of the chiral order parameter, providing a tool for experimental detecting of unconventional pairing in superconductors.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes the anomalous acoustoelectric effect as an electrical probe of chiral p-wave pairing in two-dimensional superconductors: an acoustic wave generates a transverse DC current and boundary condensate phase difference via anisotropic quasiparticle scattering (no external magnetic field). The quasiparticle-mediated response dominates near Tc and is not suppressed by electron–hole asymmetry, making it a high-sensitivity signature of unconventional (chiral) order.
AI.method: Theoretical proposal and analysis demonstrating that anisotropic scattering of quasiparticles by an acoustic wave in a 2D chiral p-wave superconductor produces a transverse DC (anomalous) acoustoelectric current and measurable condensate phase difference; emphasis on the quasiparticle-mediated contribution near Tc and its independence from electron–hole asymmetry.
AI.tags: topology,superconductivity,chiral_p-wave,acoustoelectric,quasiparticle_transport,unconventional_pairing,two-dimensional

title: Comment on "Entropic Costs of Extracting Classical Ticks from a Quantum Clock"
comment: Comment on arXiv:2502.00096 (published journal version at https://doi.org/10.1103/5rtj-djfk)
summary: A recent Letter by Wadhia et al. reports a realization of a quantum clock using a double quantum dot (DQD) [Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 200407 (2005)]. This Comment identifies two fundamental issues: (I) the claimed ``quantum clock" exhibits only classical behavior and lacks intrinsic temporal correlations between ticks; it is not sufficient for accurate time as a good clock. (II) the thermodynamic analysis misassigns entropy production and conflates amplification with measurement; the reported combined entropy is an engineering dissipation, not a fundamental cost of quantum timekeeping.

AI.tldr: TL;DR: The Comment argues the reported double-quantum-dot “quantum clock” is actually classical (no intrinsic temporal correlations between ticks) and thus inadequate as a true clock, and that the thermodynamic accounting misassigns entropy—conflating amplification/engineering dissipation with a fundamental cost of quantum timekeeping.
AI.method: The paper is a theoretical Comment/critique that analyzes the original Letter’s claims: (i) conceptual analysis of the device’s operational statistics to show absence of intrinsic temporal correlations and classical behavior; (ii) thermodynamic bookkeeping critique distinguishing fundamental entropy production from engineering amplification/dissipation and measurement versus amplification.
AI.tags: quantum_devices,measurement,thermodynamics,entropy,classicality,timekeeping

title: Superconductivity in doped spin multimer systems
summary: Binding energy, which quantifies pair formation, is a key factor in the emergence of superconductivity. Here, we show that even when multiple spins are complexly coupled, hole-doped systems, which can be mapped onto the universal hardcore boson model in the strong-binding-energy limit, exhibit promising signatures of superconductivity. We analytically and numerically demonstrate this concept in the double Kondo lattice model. Using the density-matrix renormalization group method, we show that a pairing state is maintained via a crossover even for parameters away from the strong-coupling regime. Additionally, we find that once binding energies are sufficiently generated, pair correlations develop similarly regardless of the details of local spin correlations. Our findings suggest useful guidelines for research on superconductivity.

AI.tldr: Hole-doped, strongly bound systems that map onto a universal hardcore-boson model can sustain superconducting pair formation; demonstrated in a double Kondo lattice where analytic mapping and DMRG show a pairing state persists via a crossover away from strict strong-coupling, and pair correlations emerge once binding energy is generated regardless of local spin-detail.
AI.method: Analytic mapping to the universal hardcore-boson model in the strong-binding-energy limit, plus numerical density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations on the double Kondo lattice to track pairing, crossovers, and correlation behavior.
AI.tags: superconductivity,hardcore_boson,double_Kondo_lattice,Kondo_lattice,DMRG,binding_energy,pairing_correlations,strong_coupling

title: Spin torque driven mode hybridization and band engineering in nanopatterned magnonic crystals
summary: Spin wave propagation and dynamic control are essential for reconfigurable magnonic and spintronic devices. Here, tunable mode coupling and band hybridisation are demonstrated in a nanopatterned bicomponent magnonic crystal consisting of a Permalloy/heavy metal bilayer patterned with a two dimensional array of Co nanodots. Using the plane wave method and the linearised Landau Lifshitz equation with a field like torque term, we show that inhomogeneous current induced spin torque produces periodic modulation of the magnonic frequency, enabling dynamic control of spin-wave dispersion. A pronounced avoided crossing between localised and propagating Damon Eshbach modes is observed, leading to tunable hybridisation gaps, band deformation, and enhanced mode mixing. The spin torque induced modulation enables controlled mode conversion and reconfigurable hybrid magnonic states, demonstrating efficient electrical tuning of nanoscale spin-wave dynamics.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates electrically tunable coupling and band hybridisation in a nanopatterned bicomponent magnonic crystal (Permalloy/heavy-metal bilayer with Co nanodot array). Inhomogeneous current-induced (field-like) spin torque periodically modulates magnon frequencies, producing avoided crossings between localized and propagating Damon–Eshbach modes, tunable hybridisation gaps, band deformation, and reconfigurable mode conversion at the nanoscale.
AI.method: Modeling with the plane-wave method combined with the linearised Landau–Lifshitz equation including a field-like (current-induced) torque term to capture spatially inhomogeneous spin-torque modulation of the magnonic band structure and mode hybridisation.
AI.tags: magnonic_crystal, spin_wave, spin_orbit_torque, mode_hybridisation, Damon_Eshbach, band_structure, quantum_devices

title: Fabrication and transfer of ultra-thin YBa$2$Cu$3$O$_{7-x}$ film on SrTiO$_3$ nanomembrane
summary: The fabrication of free-standing ultra-thin films from high-temperature (high-Tc) superconductors is of great interest for the development of superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors with high operating temperatures. We successfully fabricate a millimeter-sized, high-quality, ultra-thin YBa$2$Cu$3$O$_{7-x}$ (YBCO) film on an SrTiO$_3$/Sr$_{1.5}$Ca$_{1.5}$Al$_2$O$_6$ (STO/SCAO) bilayer using high-pressure sputtering. The STO nanomembranes with the YBCO films are released by dissolving the water-soluble SCAO sacrificial layer and transferred onto the SiO2/Si substrate. X-ray diffraction confirms that STO and YBCO crystallinity is preserved following transfer onto SiO2/Si substrates. Microbridges patterned from the transferred YBCO films exhibit a critical temperature of 88.8 K and a critical current density of 6.8 MA/cm2 at 77 K, demonstrating robust superconducting transport after transfer. The thermal boundary conductance across the van der Waals interface between the STO nanomembrane with YBCO film and the SiO2/Si substrate, measured over 15-75 K, is significantly reduced compared to that of epitaxial YBCO film on bulk STO leading to modified energy relaxation and enhanced stability of transient resistive states. These results establish ultra-thin YBCO films on optically transparent STO nanomembranes as a platform for integrating high-Tc superconducting devices with SiO2/Si-based photonic structures.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of millimeter-scale, ultra-thin YBa2Cu3O7-x films grown by high-pressure sputtering on STO/SCAO bilayers, released as STO nanomembranes and transferred onto SiO2/Si while retaining crystallinity and robust superconducting transport (Tc=88.8 K, Jc=6.8 MA/cm2 at 77 K). Thermal boundary conductance across the van‑der‑Waals interface to SiO2/Si is strongly reduced (15–75 K), altering energy relaxation and stabilizing transient resistive states—establishing a platform for integrating high‑Tc superconducting devices with Si photonics.
AI.method: High‑pressure sputtering growth of YBCO on an STO/SCAO bilayer, chemical release of STO nanomembranes by dissolving the water‑soluble SCAO sacrificial layer, transfer of the STO+YBCO membrane onto SiO2/Si, structural characterization (XRD) and transport measurements of patterned microbridges; thermal boundary conductance measured across the van‑der‑Waals interface over 15–75 K.
AI.tags: high-Tc, YBCO, nanomembrane, van_der_Waals_interface, thermal_boundary_conductance, superconducting_nanowire_detectors, photonic_integration, quantum_devices

title: Nonlinear Photonic Tripartite Phase
summary: Anderson localization is usually understood as a transition between extended and localized phases, with criticality confined to a single mobility edge. Recent advances predict that quasiperiodic systems can instead host a finite critical window bounded by mobility edges, in which localized, critical and extended states coexist. Yet both the experimental realization of this regime and whether interactions can provide controlled access to it remain unknown. Here, we realize such a tripartite phase in a nonlinear quasiperiodic photonic lattice and show that Kerr nonlinearity, acting as an effective interaction, enables state-selective access to the critical window. By tracking wavepacket dynamics, we distinguish localized, critical and extended transport regimes and uncover a state-selective response: rather than simply reinforcing localization through self-trapping, weak nonlinearity drives low-energy localized states into the critical window, whereas stronger nonlinearity restores localization. By contrast, critical, extended and high-energy localized states evolve monotonically towards self-trapped behaviour. Our results reveal a state-selective mechanism by which interactions provide controlled access to a pre-existing critical window in quasiperiodic systems.

AI.tldr: Experimentally demonstrates a tripartite phase (coexisting localized, critical and extended states) in a nonlinear quasiperiodic photonic lattice; Kerr nonlinearity acts as an effective interaction that enables state-selective tuning into and out of a pre-existing critical window, tracked via wavepacket dynamics.
AI.method: Experimental realization in a nonlinear quasiperiodic photonic lattice with controlled Kerr nonlinearity; characterization via time-resolved wavepacket dynamics to separate localized, critical and extended transport and to observe state-dependent nonlinear response (weak nonlinearity delocalizes low-energy localized states into the critical window; stronger nonlinearity induces self-trapping).
AI.tags: quasiperiodic, Anderson_localization, mobility_edge, critical_window, Kerr_nonlinearity, photonic_lattice, nonlinear_interactions, wavepacket_dynamics

title: Current-driven reduction of topological protection in multichannel superconductors
summary: We investigate the robustness of topological phases in a Kitaev ladder composed of two coupled superconducting chains under the perturbing influence of a finite charge current. By introducing an effective Hamiltonian depending on the quasiparticle momentum induced by the current, we show that the two-mode topological phase, present in the isolated ladder, is fragile against a finite current flux. To characterize this behavior, we combine bulk topological invariants with real-space diagnostics, including the edge-edge quantum conditional mutual information Iee, which provides an entanglement-based signature of topological order. Our results provide an effective framework to describe how current injection and measurement processes can affect topological protection in superconducting nanostructures.

AI.tldr: A two-mode topological phase in a Kitaev ladder is destabilized by a finite charge current: incorporating current as a quasiparticle-momentum shift in an effective Hamiltonian, the authors find that bulk invariants and an entanglement-based real-space diagnostic (edge–edge quantum conditional mutual information Iee) both signal loss of topological protection under finite current flux.
AI.method: Derive an effective Hamiltonian that encodes quasiparticle momentum induced by an applied charge current; evaluate bulk topological invariants and real-space entanglement diagnostics (notably the edge–edge quantum conditional mutual information Iee) for the Kitaev ladder to diagnose stability of the two-mode topological phase.
AI.tags: topology, superconductivity, Kitaev_ladder, Majorana, entanglement, quantum_devices, current-induced_decoherence

title: Direct observation of the transverse near field of an edge excitation and associated slow secondary dynamics in a fractional quantum Hall state
summary: We report stroboscopic time-resolved photoluminescence (PL) microscopy and spectroscopy revealing the transverse near field of an edge excitation in a $ν=1/3$ fractional quantum Hall (FQH) state. Time-resolved $y$-$t$ maps reveal an immediate PL response extending more than $30~μ\mathrm{m}$ into the bulk transverse to the edge when the edge magnetoplasmon (EMP) passes the mesa boundary. The nearly instantaneous nature of this long-range response identifies it as the non-radiative, quasi-electrostatic near field, revealing the EMP as a spatially extended collective excitation rather than a strictly one-dimensional charge-density oscillation. We also observe secondary bulk-side responses distinct from the immediate transverse near-field response. The coexistence of these immediate and secondary responses shows that electrically launched edge excitations produce bulk-side dynamics on widely separated time scales.

AI.tldr: Stroboscopic time‑resolved photoluminescence imaging of a ν=1/3 fractional quantum Hall edge reveals an immediate, non‑radiative quasi‑electrostatic near‑field that extends >30 μm into the bulk when an edge magnetoplasmon (EMP) passes the mesa boundary, showing the EMP is a spatially extended collective excitation; distinct, slower secondary bulk responses are also observed, indicating multi‑timescale bulk dynamics triggered by electrically launched edge excitations.
AI.method: Stroboscopic time‑resolved photoluminescence (PL) microscopy and spectroscopy producing y–t maps of the transverse PL response to electrically launched edge magnetoplasmons in a ν=1/3 fractional quantum Hall mesa, distinguishing immediate near‑field (quasi‑electrostatic) signals from secondary delayed bulk responses.
AI.tags: fractional_quantum_Hall, edge_magnetoplasmon, near_field, time_resolved_photoluminescence, collective_excitation, bulk_dynamics

title: Topological semimetals: surface transport and spin effects
summary: For the solid state physics, recent interest to topological systems is mostly connected with topological semimetals, in particular, to Weyl ones as the most representative semimetal type. Like other topological materials, e.g. topological and Chern insulators, topological semimetals acquire topologically protected surface states with linear dispersion. In contrast to helical surface states in topological insulators, the surface states are chiral for Weyl semimetals, similarly to Chern insulators, which allows to consider Weyl semimetals as the three-dimensional analog of the quantum Hall effect regime. Weyl semimetals are also interesting for spin-dependent effects, due to the spin-momentum locking in the topological surface states. For topological semimetals, the main problem of transport investigations is to reveal the surface states contribution in the material with gapless bulk spectrum. Here, we present review of experimental results on charge and spin transport in topological semimetals: charge transport in different superconducting proximity devices; spin-dependent transport; magnetic response of the topological surface states; non-linear anomalous Hall effect as the direct manifestation of the non-zero Berry curvature in topological semimetals. Possible applications are also considered for this new class of topological materials.

AI.tldr: Review of experimental charge and spin transport in topological semimetals (primarily Weyl), assessing how chiral topological surface states manifest in transport despite gapless bulk; surveys superconducting-proximity devices, spin-dependent transport, magnetic response of surface states, and nonlinear anomalous Hall measurements (Berry-curvature effects) and discusses potential applications.
AI.method: Literature review synthesizing experimental transport and magneto-transport studies: superconducting-proximity devices, spin-resolved and magnetotransport measurements of surface states, and nonlinear Hall measurements as probes of Berry curvature.
AI.tags: topology, quantum_geometry, spin_transport, superconducting_proximity, Weyl_semimetal, nonlinear_anomalous_Hall

title: Gyromagnetic Quantum Friction in Rayleigh Vorticity Baths
summary: We identify an intrinsic zero-temperature relaxation channel for near-surface spins gyromagnetically coupled to Rayleigh-wave vorticity. This surface-mode contribution requires no thermal phonons, unlike Raman relaxation, and is fixed by Rayleigh vorticity rather than material-specific $g$-factor modulation. The Rayleigh-vorticity bath is super-Ohmic and evanescent with depth, producing field and depth scalings of spin relaxation. These scalings establish shallow spin sensors and hybrid surface-acoustic-wave spin interfaces as detectors of Rayleigh-wave acoustic quantum friction in solids.

AI.tldr: Near-surface electronic spins experience an intrinsic zero-temperature relaxation channel arising from gyromagnetic coupling to the vorticity of Rayleigh (surface acoustic) waves. This mechanism requires no thermal phonons, is set by Rayleigh vorticity rather than g-factor modulation, and produces super‑Ohmic, depth‑evanescent spectral properties that yield characteristic field and depth scalings. Implications include using shallow spin sensors and hybrid SAW–spin interfaces to detect acoustic quantum friction.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis identifying gyromagnetic coupling between near-surface spins and Rayleigh-wave vorticity, characterization of the Rayleigh-vorticity bath as super‑Ohmic and evanescent with depth, derivation of resulting field and depth scalings for spin relaxation, and proposal of sensing/interfaces to detect Rayleigh-wave acoustic quantum friction.
AI.tags: vortex, surface_acoustic_wave, Rayleigh_wave, spin_relaxation, super-Ohmic_bath, acoustic_friction, quantum_devices

title: Quantum Batteries in two-dimensional material-based Josephson Junctions
summary: We investigate the solid-state implementation of a Dicke-like quantum battery consisting of a two-dimensional material-based Josephson junction inductively coupled to a resonator, using graphene as a representative example. In this configuration, Andreev bound states naturally act as non-interacting, energetically non-degenerate two-level systems, and the setup allows for both single-photon and two-photon resonant processes. The coupling between the LC-circuit flux and the supercurrent through the junction gives rise to peculiar longitudinal interaction terms that have no counterpart in the conventional Dicke model. These additional couplings can enhance energy storage for a proper range of parameters. The proposed architecture also enables an alternative, but equivalent, charging protocol that relies on tuning the superconducting phase difference across the junction.

AI.tldr: Proposal and theoretical analysis of a solid-state Dicke-like quantum battery: a 2D-material (graphene) Josephson junction inductively coupled to an LC resonator, where Andreev bound states act as non-interacting, non-degenerate two-level systems. Flux–supercurrent coupling produces longitudinal interaction terms beyond the conventional Dicke model that can enhance charging; charging can be done via photon drives or by tuning the superconducting phase difference.
AI.method: Modeling of a Josephson-junction–LC resonator hybrid (graphene-based junction as representative) treating Andreev bound states as two-level systems; identification and derivation of single- and two-photon resonant processes and additional longitudinal coupling terms arising from flux–supercurrent interaction; parameter-space analysis showing regimes where these extra couplings boost energy storage; proposal of an equivalent charging protocol based on phase-bias control.
AI.tags: quantum_devices, superconductivity, Josephson_junction, Andreev_bound_states, Dicke_model, circuit_QED, two_photon_processes, phase_control

title: Quasinormal mode quantization of bound and propagating photons in complex lightguiding nanostructures for integrated devices
summary: Open optical or plasmonic resonators are placed on and connected through surfaces or via waveguides, forming complex lightguiding nanostructures, e.g. for integrated photonic quantum devices. We derive general boundary conditions for quasinormal modes that account for the structure's specific geometry. We then present a general quantization scheme for multiple, interacting quasinormal-mode cavities coupled to quantum emitters and to a non-bosonic bath of propagating photons on waveguides or a surface. We derive a system-bath Hamiltonian with rigorously defined coupling elements that can be computed using Maxwell solvers, including light-matter coupling between the electromagnetic field and quantum emitters. We define system-bath correlation functions for an effective, bath-mediated, and time-delayed interaction between the quasinormal modes and quantum emitters, which is a main ingredient commonly used to simulate open quantum system dynamics.

AI.tldr: Provides a rigorous quantization framework for networks of open optical/plasmonic resonators: derives quasinormal-mode (QNM) boundary conditions for arbitrary connected geometries and constructs a system–bath Hamiltonian for multiple interacting QNMs coupled to quantum emitters and a non‑bosonic bath of propagating photons, with coupling matrix elements computable from Maxwell solvers and bath-mediated, time‑delayed correlation functions for open-system dynamics.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of general QNM boundary conditions for resonators connected via surfaces or waveguides; formulation of a quantization scheme yielding a system–bath Hamiltonian with explicitly defined coupling elements (including light–matter coupling) that can be evaluated using electromagnetic (Maxwell) solvers; definition of system–bath correlation functions to capture bath‑mediated, time‑delayed interactions.
AI.tags: quantum_devices, quantum_computing, quasinormal_modes, waveguides, light-matter_coupling, system-bath, open_quantum_systems, photonics

title: Nonlinear frequency shift and bistability of magnon-polarons
summary: We investigate the nonlinear dynamics of strongly coupled surface acoustic waves (SAWs) and spin waves (SWs) in a magnetoacoustic resonator based on a YIG/ZnO heterostructure by combining microwave reflection measurements with microfocused Brillouin light scattering spectroscopy. In the linear regime, the electrical response reveals clear hybridization between standing SAW cavity modes and finite-wave-vector SWs, resulting in pronounced avoided crossings. At elevated drive powers, the hybrid system exhibits a strongly field-dependent nonlinear response characterized by a positive frequency shift of the driven SW mode. Using the vector Hamiltonian formalism for nonlinear spin-wave dynamics, we show that this shift is dominated by a cross-shift term. In our resonator geometry, this contribution becomes significant because the standing SAW cavity mode simultaneously excites counterpropagating SWs with wave vectors $+k$ and $-k$. For suitable field detuning, the nonlinear shift drives the SW mode into resonance with the SAW excitation, leading to a strong enhancement of the magnon population, broadband nonlinear scattering, and bistable foldover behavior. Beyond the foldover threshold, both the magnon and phonon responses stabilize. These results establish SAW-driven $k \neq 0$ magnon-phonon hybrids as a promising platform for nonlinear magnetoacoustics and wave-based information processing.

AI.tldr: Strong coupling between standing SAW cavity modes and finite-k spin waves in a YIG/ZnO resonator produces pronounced avoided crossings in the linear regime; at high drive power a cross-shift (from simultaneous +k and -k SW excitation) causes a positive nonlinear SW frequency shift that can bring the magnon into resonance with the SAW, producing large magnon population, broadband nonlinear scattering, bistable foldover and eventual stabilization of magnon and phonon responses. This establishes SAW-driven k≠0 magnon–phonon hybrids as a platform for nonlinear magnetoacoustics and wave-based information processing.
AI.method: Experimental: microwave reflection measurements combined with microfocused Brillouin light scattering spectroscopy on a YIG/ZnO SAW resonator; theoretical modeling via a vector Hamiltonian formalism for nonlinear spin-wave dynamics identifying a dominant cross-shift term from counterpropagating SWs.
AI.tags: magnon-phonon_coupling, surface_acoustic_waves, spin_waves, nonlinear_dynamics, magnetoacoustics, bistability, YIG_ZnO, quantum_devices

title: Topologically Driven Giant Effective Spin Mixing Conductance in Antiferromagnetic FeSn/Py Heterostructures
summary: The topological semimetal FeSn antiferromagnet, characterized by its kagome lattice, two-dimensional flat bands, and Dirac-like surface states, holds immense promise for spintronic applications. In this work, for the first time, we investigate the spin pumping behavior in epitaxial-FeSn/Py (Ni$_{80}$Fe$_{20}$) heterostructures. We report a giant effective spin mixing conductance (g$^{\uparrow \downarrow}_{\mathrm{eff}}$) of $(116\pm 7)$~nm$^{-2}$, which is nearly one order of magnitude higher than that of standard Pt/Py heterostructures. The insertion of a 3 nm Al spacer layer results in a two-fold reduction in the effective damping, confirming the interfacial origin of the large g$^{\uparrow\downarrow}_{\mathrm{eff}}$. Consistently, we observe an order-of-magnitude higher inverse spin Hall effect voltage in the FeSn/Py system compared to a reference Pt/Py film stack. We attribute the giant g$^{\uparrow\downarrow}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ to the direct interfacing of the Py layer with the topologically active [001]-kagome surface of epitaxial-FeSn. These findings establish the critical role of topologically active interfaces for advanced quantum-material-based spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: Epitaxial FeSn/Py heterostructures exhibit a giant effective spin mixing conductance g_eff=(116±7) nm^{-2}—≈10× larger than Pt/Py—and an order‑of‑magnitude larger inverse spin Hall voltage; inserting a 3 nm Al spacer halves the additional damping, implicating a topologically active [001] kagome FeSn/Py interface as the origin.
AI.method: Experimental spin‑pumping study using epitaxial FeSn/Ni80Fe20 (Py) heterostructures: ferromagnetic resonance/damping extraction to obtain g^{↑↓}_{eff}, inverse spin Hall voltage measurements for spin‑to‑charge conversion, spacer‑layer (3 nm Al) insertion and Pt/Py reference stacks for interfacial control and comparison.
AI.tags: topology, spintronics, spin_pumping, spin_mixing_conductance, inverse_spin_Hall, kagome, topological_surface_states, FeSn, interfaces, quantum_devices

title: Quantum-metric Bloch oscillations in weakly inhomogeneous electric fields
summary: Geometric analogs of Bloch oscillations studied so far have relied on Berry curvature. We show that a weakly inhomogeneous electric field adds a distinct quantum-metric term to semiclassical wavepacket dynamics, generating an oscillatory real-space contribution even when the Berry curvature vanishes. The associated transport response comprises an intrinsic and a scattering-time-dependent part. In the regime studied, the latter can dominate and approach finite saturation at high field when the relative field inhomogeneity is held fixed. A tilted Dirac model illustrates the mechanism. Realistic platforms will likely require synthetically engineered superlattices, with a finite quantum metric and an adequate band gap.

AI.tldr: Weak spatial inhomogeneity in an applied electric field produces a quantum‑metric contribution to semiclassical wavepacket dynamics that yields oscillatory real‑space motion even when Berry curvature = 0. The induced transport has an intrinsic part and a scattering‑time‑dependent part that can dominate and saturate at large fields; mechanism is demonstrated in a tilted Dirac model and realistic realization likely needs engineered superlattices with finite quantum metric and a band gap.
AI.method: Semiclassical wavepacket dynamics extended to include weak electric‑field inhomogeneity, deriving a quantum‑metric term in the equations of motion; analytic decomposition of transport response into intrinsic and scattering‑time‑dependent contributions; demonstration via a tilted Dirac model and discussion of experimental platform requirements (superlattices, finite quantum metric, band gap).
AI.tags: quantum_geometry, wavepacket_semiclassics, Berry_curvature, transport, tilted_Dirac_model, superlattice

title: Transport Enhancement and In Situ Control of Electronic Correlation via Photoinduced Modulation Doping of van der Waals Heterostructures
summary: Modulation doping, a well-established technique for traditional semiconductor heterostructures, is a promising approach for tailoring carrier concentration in 2D materials devices. In this letter we report on photoinduced modulation doping in hBN-graphene-hBN-SiO2 heterostructures utilizing standard white light sources and no additional fabrication complexity. We establish the use of this technique to both dope the channel material and to photoanneal devices, providing control over electronic doping and disorder in the graphene channel. We analyze the transport properties by employing Drude and Landauer transport models, highlighting the ability to reversibly tune the mobility and mean scattering length of the graphene with a high degree of accuracy. This tunability allows us to switch our device between the diffusive and quasi-ballistic transport regimes in situ. We utilize the exceptional control our technique provides over local disorder to realize quantum Hall isospin ferromagnetic states in a device whose initial quality would otherwise leave such states unobservable. These results demonstrate precise manipulation of carrier density and charge disorder in van der Waals heterostructures, providing a highly accessible approach to creating high-quality devices capable of realizing correlated electronic states.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of photoinduced modulation doping in hBN–graphene–hBN–SiO2 heterostructures using standard white light to reversibly control carrier density and charge disorder, enabling in situ switching between diffusive and quasi‑ballistic transport and recovery of quantum Hall isospin ferromagnetic states in otherwise low‑quality devices.
AI.method: Optical (white‑light) photoinduced modulation doping and photoannealing of hBN‑encapsulated graphene (no added fabrication steps); transport characterization and parameter extraction using Drude and Landauer models to quantify mobility and mean scattering length and to track reversible tuning of disorder and transport regime.

title: Entanglement Dynamics across a Monitored Quantum Point Contact
summary: We compute the entanglement dynamics across a monitored quantum point contact, where particle losses are recorded on a given site, and demonstrate how this single-site local monitoring substantially reshapes the entanglement production. Contrary to the unitary case, where entanglement entropy grows logarithmically in time, here we find first a linear growth, up to a maximum value displaying volume-law scaling, and then a slow decay to zero, as the system empties out. We capture this crossover using a quasiparticle picture, where the first linear growth arises due to an emergent bias voltage established by the losses, which eventually decays away as the system depletes. We connect our results to studies of the Page curve and to experimentally relevant probes, via full counting statistics of charge transfer across a subregion, with only a single channel to unravel leading to a favorable scaling of the postselection overhead. Natural platforms for this setting include mesoscopic systems and ultracold atoms.

AI.tldr: Monitoring single-site particle losses at a quantum point contact qualitatively alters entanglement production: instead of unitary logarithmic growth, entanglement exhibits an initial linear increase up to a volume-law maximum and then a slow decay to zero as the system empties. A quasiparticle picture explains this via an emergent, transient bias induced by losses; results are tied to Page-curve ideas and probed via full counting statistics.
AI.method: The study computes entanglement dynamics for a monitored quantum point contact with particle losses recorded on a single site, combining explicit calculation of entanglement entropy and full counting statistics with a quasiparticle semiclassical picture that captures the crossover (loss-induced emergent bias → system depletion). Connections to Page-curve phenomenology and experimentally relevant probes are established.
AI.tags: measurement-induced_entanglement, entanglement_dynamics, quantum_point_contact, full_counting_statistics, Page_curve, quasiparticle_picture, monitored_quantum_systems, quantum_devices, ultracold_atoms, mesoscopic_systems

title: Spintronic Neuromorphic Hardware Using Domain Wall Based Neurons and Quantized Synapses
summary: In this work, we simulate the functionality of artificial neuron and synapse using spin-orbit torque-based spintronic devices and implemented a fully connected artificial neural netwrok (ANN). These neuro-synaptic devices are emulated using transverse domain wall dynamics in a rectangular magnetic nanotrack comprised of heavy metal/ferromagnet (HM/FM) heterostructures. The ReLU activation function of the neuron has been mimicked using the domain wall motion induced by a 3 ns current pulse. The synapse has been modelled using current-induced domain wall (DW) dynamics through a corrugated HM/FM nanotrack under the influence of a 10 ns current pulse with varying current density. The semicircular corrugations are in the form of notches, which are symmetrically located on both sides of the nanotrack. By applying 10 ns current pulses of varying densities, we achieve controlled DW pinning, revealing a step-like motion caused by temporary pauses at each pinning center. The electrical conductance of the pinned DW across various pinning points, act as stable synaptic weights for our ANN. Furthermore, we observe a threshold-dependent delay effect where each depinning event is influenced by previous ones, successfully mimicking synaptic memory and adaptability in neuromorphic systems. The fully connected ANN has been modeled using the conventional float32 synaptic weights for the MNIST and Fashion MNIST datasets with an accuracy of ~97 % and ~86 %, respectively, which serves as a test bed of our neuromorphic simulations. With the aim of implementing a sparse and low memory footprint ANN, we quantize the trained synaptic weights into discrete quantized level and tested the network, which demonstrate an accuracy of ~95% and ~62%, for the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST dataset, respectively.

AI.tldr: Authors simulate spintronic neuromorphic elements where transverse domain-wall (DW) motion in heavy-metal/ferromagnet nanotracks (with semicircular notch corrugations) implements neuron (ReLU via 3 ns pulse) and synapse (stepwise, pinning-mediated conductance states via 10 ns pulses). DW pinning/depinning produces stable, discrete conductance levels as synaptic weights and a history-dependent depinning delay that mimics synaptic memory. They test a fully connected ANN on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST achieving ~97%/~86% with float32 weights and ~95%/~62% after quantizing weights.
AI.method: Numerical simulation of spin-orbit-torque-driven transverse domain-wall dynamics in corrugated HM/FM nanotracks to emulate neuron activation (short pulses) and synaptic weight storage (pinning at notches); mapping pinned-DW conductances to ANN weights and evaluating classification performance (including weight quantization) on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST.
AI.tags: spintronics, spin-orbit_torque, domain_wall_dynamics, neuromorphic, machine_learning, quantum_devices, synaptic_weights, MNIST

title: Monitored quantum transport through a disordered one-dimensional conductor
summary: We formulate a quantum master equation for the many-particle density matrix of electrons propagating through a single-mode conductor, combining elastic scattering by disorder with time-resolved projective measurements that monitor the outcome of scattering events. The full counting statistics of transmitted electrons has a binomial distribution function, whose mean ${\cal T}$ and variance ${\cal T}(1-{\cal T})$ determine the conductance and shot noise power, respectively. Monitoring suppresses the phase coherence responsible for one-dimensional localization: The decay with conductor length $L$ of the typical transmission probability crosses over at $L\simeq \ell_φ$ from the exponential $e^{-L/ξ}$ (with localization length $ξ$) to the Ohmic $1/L$ decay. Numerical solution of the master equation gives, for weak monitoring, a logarithmic dependence $\ell_φ\simeq ξ\ln(v_{\rm F}τ_φ/ξ)$ of the coherence length $\ell_φ$ on the mean time $τ_φ$ between measurements.

AI.tldr: Derives a quantum master equation for the many-particle density matrix of electrons in a single‑mode disordered conductor subject to time‑resolved projective measurements. Monitoring yields binomial full counting statistics (mean T, variance T(1−T)), suppresses 1D Anderson localization so transmission vs length L crosses over at L≈ℓ_φ from exponential e^{−L/ξ} to Ohmic 1/L, and for weak monitoring the coherence length scales as ℓ_φ ≃ ξ ln(v_F τ_φ/ξ).
AI.method: Construct a quantum master equation combining elastic scattering by static disorder with stochastic/projective time‑resolved measurements of scattering outcomes; compute full counting statistics and transmission statistics analytically and by numerical solution of the master equation to extract decay laws and the dependence of the monitoring‑induced coherence length ℓ_φ on the mean measurement interval τ_φ.
AI.tags: quantum_master_equation,measurement-induced_decoherence,full_counting_statistics,Anderson_localization,shot_noise,single-mode_conductor,quantum_devices

title: Signatures of quantum chaos in phonon-polariton billiards
summary: We use scanning near-field optical microscopy to image hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) billiards with integrable and chaotic geometries. In Sinai billiards, we observe irregular mode patterns consistent with quantum scarring, together with an unexpected sensitivity to weak probe perturbations. These random-wave features coexist with non-chaotic one-dimensional boundary modes arising from nontrivial polariton reflection at the billiard edge. As the billiard boundary becomes increasingly complex, the Fourier transforms of the measured signals evolve toward ring-like structures consistent with Berry's random-wave conjecture. We develop a numerical framework based on the Helmholtz equation with generalized boundary conditions that encode angle-dependent reflection phase shifts. The calculated level statistics exhibit a crossover from Poisson-like behavior in integrable billiards to Wigner-Dyson-like behavior in chaotic geometries, with small deviations from the canonical form arising from nonlinear boundary conditions that require self-consistent bulk-boundary analysis. Theoretical analysis based on dissipative Green's functions qualitatively reproduces the near-field data. These results establish mesoscopic van der Waals billiards as a rich platform for studying generalized chaotic dynamics of hybrid light-matter polaritons.

AI.tldr: Scanning near-field optical microscopy of hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hBN billiards reveals coexistence of chaotic (Sinai-like) random-wave/scarred modes and non‑chaotic one‑dimensional boundary modes; Fourier-space statistics approach Berry’s random‑wave limit as boundaries become complex. Numerical Helmholtz simulations with angle‑dependent reflection phases and dissipative Green’s‑function theory reproduce a crossover in level statistics from Poisson‑like to Wigner‑Dyson‑like behaviour with deviations due to nonlinear, self‑consistent bulk–boundary conditions.
AI.method: Experiment: scattering-type scanning near‑field optical microscopy (SNOM) imaging and spatial Fourier analysis of hyperbolic phonon polariton modes in patterned hBN billiards. Theory/numerics: Helmholtz equation with generalized (angle‑dependent) boundary conditions encoding polariton reflection phase shifts; level‑statistics analysis; dissipative Green’s‑function calculations to model near‑field response.

title: Signatures of the Quantum Geometric Dipole of Interlayer Excitons in Counterflow Conductivity
summary: Collective excitations of many-body electron systems can carry internal structure, supporting novel quantum geometric and topological properties. Among these are a quantum geometric dipole (QGD), which for excitons have direct significance as an internal polarization. For interlayer excitons of a bilayer system, this represents an in-plane dipole moment, which can be used to drive them with in-plane electric fields. In this work, we consider counterflow electric currents associated with driven excitons in such a bilayer system as a probe of their QGD structure. As a simple but non-trivial example, we analyze a structure with a one-dimensional periodic potential in a strong perpendicular magnetic field. The resulting magnetoexciton bands host QGD structure that distinguishes it from the exciton QGD of a uniform system. To model exciton transport we adopt a Boltzmann approach that includes inter-band tunneling, allowing us to consider non-equilibrium momentum distributions that result from strong layer-antisymmetric driving fields. We show how linear response to a layer-symmetric component of the driving fields provide information about the QGD, and that the broad QGD structure of the exciton bands can be probed by the varying the layer-antisymmetric field. Our results demonstrate that counterflow conductivity serves as a tunable probe of the internal quantum geometric structure carried by the interlayer excitons, connecting transport to the quantum geometry of many-body excitations.

AI.tldr: Counterflow conductivity of driven interlayer excitons in a bilayer with a 1D periodic potential and strong perpendicular magnetic field can be used to probe the excitons' quantum geometric dipole (QGD). The paper derives magnetoexciton bands with nontrivial QGD and shows — via a semiclassical Boltzmann transport treatment that includes inter-band tunneling and layer-antisymmetric driving — how linear-response counterflow signatures (to layer-symmetric fields) and their tuning by layer-antisymmetric fields reveal the excitons' internal quantum geometry.
AI.method: The authors build magnetoexciton bandstructures for a bilayer with a one-dimensional periodic potential in a strong B-field, compute the exciton QGD distribution, and model exciton transport using a semiclassical Boltzmann equation including inter-band tunneling to obtain non-equilibrium momentum distributions under layer-antisymmetric driving; they analyze linear-response counterflow conductivity to extract QGD signatures.
AI.tags: quantum_geometry, interlayer_excitons, magnetoexciton, counterflow_conductivity, Boltzmann_transport, interband_tunneling, bilayer_systems
